analysis.one_liner: Imposes new rules on pharmacy benefit managers in Medicare and employer health plans.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in September 2026 and referred to three House committees; no vote or hearing has taken place.
analysis.plain_summary: Pharmacy benefit managers are the middlemen that employers and Medicare pay to negotiate drug prices and manage pharmacy benefits. Their fees and pricing practices are widely blamed for pushing drug costs up for patients and plans. This bill would put new requirements on those middlemen under Medicare (title XVIII of the Social Security Act) and under employer health plans governed by the 1974 employee benefits law. It has not advanced past its initial committee referrals.
analysis.who_benefits: If it passes, Medicare beneficiaries and people with employer health coverage would benefit to the extent the new requirements lower out-of-pocket drug costs or pharmacy reimbursement cuts. Independent pharmacies, which often lose money when benefit managers under-reimburse them, would also gain.

how_it_helps.text: The bill targets pharmacy benefit managers under Medicare and employer plans, the two channels through which most Americans get their medicines.
Requirements on these middlemen are aimed at practices that add costs between the drug maker and the patient.

analysis.who_pays: Pharmacy benefit managers, the large companies that negotiate drug prices and manage pharmacy networks for insurers, employers, and Medicare, would bear the cost of complying with the new rules, and drug makers could see their negotiated arrangements with those middlemen change.

drawbacks.text: The bill text is not available in the provided record, so the actual strength of the new requirements — whether they simply require disclosure or actually cap fees and pricing spreads — cannot be confirmed from the sources provided.
Stronger rules on middlemen could reduce the rebates that benefit managers say keep list prices and premiums down, a trade-off their industry typically raises against reform bills.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: If the requirements are real rather than disclosure-only, the likely benefit — lower drug costs for patients and fairer payment to pharmacies — outweighs compliance costs concentrated in a small number of large middleman companies. But with the bill text not provided, its actual strength can't be verified, and it has shown no movement since introduction.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to three House committees, and none of them has taken it up yet.

narrative.text: Representative Ryan Mackenzie, a Republican from Pennsylvania, introduced the bill on September 14, 2026.

The Speaker referred it to the Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Education and Workforce Committees, which is what happens when a bill touches several committee jurisdictions; it has not received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote in any of them.
Four members cosponsored it: two Democrats and two Republicans.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: With nothing enacted yet, pharmacy benefit managers continue operating under existing rules.

for.name: Rep. Ryan Mackenzie
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to impose new requirements on pharmacy benefit managers under Medicare and employer plans.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor is a Republican and cosponsors split evenly between two Democrats and two Republicans; no member has opposed it, and no committee has acted on it yet.

industries.note: These middleman companies sit between drug makers, insurers, and pharmacies and profit from fees and pricing practices the bill would subject to new requirements. Stronger rules could shrink their margins.
Pharmacies are often paid less by benefit managers than it costs to fill prescriptions. Requirements aimed at benefit manager reimbursement and transparency would tend to help them stay open.

analysis.trajectory: A bill introduced in mid-September with four cosponsors and no committee action is unlikely to get a standalone vote before the Congress ends on January 3, 2027. Its most realistic path to a floor vote is having provisions folded into a larger health or spending package, which has happened to pharmacy benefit manager provisions in past Congresses.
